While an inventory of existing working groups is outside the scope of this chapter, in the next section we highlight three recent policy problems and solutions that required or triggered cooperation across federal, state, and Alaska Native organizations. We also evaluate each case for its fit to our conceptions of coercive and treaty federalism.

Case studies of federalist challenges Environmental assessment as a shared responsibility Under the US regime for water quality, the 1972 Clean Water Act, Alaska shares responsibility for conserving the quality of freshwater, estuarine and coastal marine ecosystems across the state. The federal government and the state collaboratively manage the regulatory requirements for reviewing, permitting, and evaluating the environmental impact of development activities that affect these water bodies. One of the most contentious development proposals facing regulators is the potential Pebble Mine. In 2007, mining giants Northern Dynasty and AngloAmerican joined in a partnership to promote the development of a potentially very large mine to excavate approximately 55 billion tons of copper, 67 million ounces of gold, and 3 billion tons of molybdenum.15 The planning site for the mine covers 28 square miles (7,252 hectares) of land that straddles two extraordinarily productive rivers, the Nushagak and Kvichak. Both rivers flow into Bristol Bay, the ecosystem that produces the top Pacific sockeye salmon fishery in the world in terms of value and pounds of wild commercial fish.16 In 2010, the fishery was worth over USD 500 million in annual income and supported 12,000 fishing and processing jobs.17 Significant numbers of Alaskan coastal communities depend on the return of salmon to create a critical economic component of household wealth. Subsistence fisheries have been valued for the amount of grocery spending that is offset by acquiring wild foods, but the value of subsistence fisheries encompasses a way of life that is complex, and the sustainability of those communities relies on the cultural connection to the environment as well as what it can provide. For its part, Northern Dynasty and Anglo-American (a corporation that later dropped its stake in the project) have also released economic data estimating that the project will produce 15,000 jobs each year, provide USD 18 billion in revenue to local, state, and federal taxes, and result in USD 64 billion in economic contributions to the US gross domestic product.18 In 2010, regional tribes and Alaska Native organizations (including the regional Bristol Bay Native Corporation) petitioned the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to conduct an ecological risk assessment of the area that would likely be disturbed by large-scale mining. The agency reports that under its assumed mine development scenarios, significant amounts of freshwater habitat for salmon and other species would be destroyed in the immediate vicinity of the mine, and downstream habitat quality would likely be diminished due to water quality impacts from mining production wastes. The assessment does note that habitat destruction could be potentially mitigated somewhat by careful siting decisions. The assessment itself is somewhat of a departure from the way that Alaska and the federal government share in the implementation of the Clean Water Act, a legal framework for governing the release of pollution (including mining wastes) into waterways and wetlands. Alaska has the authority to issue permits to allow particular developments to pollute surface waters under the Clean Water Act. However, the EPA retains the authority to review permits that Alaska issues. The size and scale of the mine, potentially the largest mining development in the world according to the EPA, motivated regional actors to ask the federal agency to prohibit large-scale mining in the area.19 Instead, the EPA performed an ecological risk assessment based on the resources in the area versus the impact of a particular mining development plan. The State of Alaska’s Departments of Natural Resource and Law expressed their disapproval of the ecological risk assessment process, arguing that the EPA lacks authority to conduct such an assessment and, ‘ ... disregards federal and state laws, processes, and permits, the Statehood Compact, as well as the Alaska Constitution’.20 The balancing act of federal and state power sharing in a case as divisive as the Pebble Mine illustrates a key challenge of federalism. Part of the tension comes from the EPA’s concurrent roles of bureaucratic oversight and evaluator of environmental justice issues with federally permitted projects. In its analysis, the agency warns of the potential environmental justice implications of the Pebble Mine if developed as assumed by the agency, ‘If salmon quality or quantity was (or was perceived to be) adversely affected, the nutritional, social, and spiritual health of Alaska Natives would decline.’21 The case reflects both types of federalism we have highlighted, coercive and treaty federalism. The EPA maintains strict oversight (more or less, depending on the administration’s priorities) but is also bound by treaty federalism to consult with tribal governments and intervene in projects that disproportionately affect minority populations. In the EPA’s final analysis, the concern for ecological and cultural values outweighed the potential for mining revenue and mining jobs as it prepared to issue rules disallowing mining wastes from entering Bristol Bay from the proposed Pebble Mine area. Industrial development of the Outer Continental Shelf The state and the federal government both support responsible development of oil and gas deposits, even as they disagree on the strategies to attain such development. Regional and national actors and voters are split on the value of oil and gas development in the Arctic, but many may not realize that the Alaskan Arctic already hosts numerous oil and gas development projects. The state has authority to permit oil and gas development within its lands and waters (up to three miles from shore), and the Northstar development complex is an example of federalist approaches to development, as both the state and the federal government were involved in the assessment and permitting process. More recently, projects put forward in Alaska’s coastal waters have been developed using horizontal drilling technology that allows producers to maintain facilities adjacent to shore, on artificial islands. This type of development has seemed more acceptable to local communities and tribal organizations, which also likely realize the determination the state has to proceed with development. The larger battles have been waged over development in federal waters, partially due to the fact that there are more avenues of legal contestation (i.e., veto points) in federal permitting schemes. Coordinating development in federal waters is now also addressed in national ocean policy and climate change adaptation strategies. The state preference is to expedite permitting of offshore development without a framework for ocean governance, as a way to maximize operational flexibility for oil and gas companies. The linkage of these three policy areas, Arctic oil and gas, ocean policy, and climate change adaptation, contrasts with the priority area the state has emphasized in policy pronouncements: economic development. This case also points toward coercive federalism in that rules relating to resources on federal lands may effectively limit economic opportunities for states. At the same time, any development that is permitted that may affect protected resources (such as marine mammals or endangered species) or that may affect the subsistence harvests of such resources by Alaska Native hunters is also carefully evaluated. The mitigation of risk to protected species and subsistence hunts are comanaged between Alaska Native organizations and federal agencies, pointing toward treaty federalism as well. State influence over Arctic policy The first federal policy to acknowledge the Arctic as a national security priority was Richard Nixon’s brief 1971 two-page National Security Decision Memorandum 144. Since then the American Arctic has been addressed in security policy through Ronald Reagan’s 1983 National Security Decision Directive 90, Bill Clinton’s 1994 Presidential Decision Directive 26, and George W. Bush’s 2009 National Security Presidential Directive 66/Homeland Security Presidential Directive 25. 22 In 2009, President Obama reaffirmed his predecessor’s Arctic policy with the following six goals: (1) meet Arctic-specific national and homeland security needs; (2) protect and conserve Arctic environments; (3) ensure the environmental sustainability of natural resource management and economic development; (4) strengthen institutions for pan-Arctic cooperation; (5) involve Arctic indigenous communities in ‘decisions that affect them’; and (6) enhance scientific monitoring and research into cross-scale environmental issues.23 The policy also states what has become a consensus view at the Arctic Council against a comprehensive treaty similar to the Antarctic Treaty but calls for the assertion of American military and police power in Arctic waters, in recognition of the geopolitics of sea ice retreat. Additionally, the policy underscores the need to secure free passage through the Northwest Passage and the Northern Sea Route.24 The Obama administration has been more proactive in Arctic issues than previous administrations, sending Secretary of State Clinton to the 2011 Arctic Council meeting in Greenland, agreeing to the 2011 Arctic Search and Rescue agreement and contributing to the Marine Oil Pollution Preparedness and Response plan, but there remain inefficiencies and bureaucratic fragmentation of efforts across agencies relating to Arctic policy.

The Commission is charged to hold a series of hearings across the state to gather the views on policy priorities of the citizens, many of whom are already living and adapting to changing conditions. Members of the Commission have also been active in meeting with US State Department task force involved in implementing the National Strategy on the Arctic Region. Part of the role of the Commission is to elevate local and regional perspectives into federal and international policy venues such as the Arctic Council.26 Like many subnational governmental actors, the Commission

The Commission’s work resulted in the introduction of an Arctic legislative initiative, including the creation of an investment fund for Arctic infrastructure, a new port authority to govern maritime facilities siting and development, and a joint resolution of the Alaska House of Representatives expressing the sentiment that the US government should consider Alaskan priorities during its chairmanship of the Arctic Council from 2015 to 2017.27 General priorities have been identified by the Governor, the Alaska Legislature, and civil society groups, but only the Legislature has undertaken a transparent public process to develop its set of priorities.
